ask.changes_what: A positive exposure history should lead to stopping or dose-adjusting the agent, avoiding further nephrotoxins and monitoring creatinine; still assess obstruction and volume status.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not attribute AKI solely to a drug or contrast when there is oliguria, sepsis, hypotension or possible obstruction; these still need evaluation.
ask.escalation_warning: AKI with hyperkalemia, acidosis, fluid overload or uremic symptoms needs urgent nephrology review regardless of the exposure history.
ask.how: Reconcile all drugs against the chart and pharmacy record, including over-the-counter NSAIDs and herbal products: NSAIDs, ACEi/ARB, diuretics, aminoglycosides, vancomycin (with piperacillin-tazobactam), PPIs, and any iodinated contrast. For each, record start date, dose change and timing relative to the creatinine rise.
ask.negative_finding: No exposure lowers the likelihood of drug-related AKI and contrast nephropathy, redirecting attention to hypovolemia, sepsis, obstruction and intrinsic renal disease.
ask.pitfalls: Patients under-report OTC NSAIDs; PPI-associated AIN can begin weeks to months after the start; contrast-associated AKI is often confounded by the illness that prompted imaging, so timing alone does not prove causation.
ask.positive_finding: A nephrotoxin started or dosed within days of the creatinine rise, or contrast within 48-72 h, makes drug-induced AKI (hemodynamic, ATN or AIN) a leading candidate and identifies an immediately reversible factor.
ask.prerequisites: Access to medication administration and imaging records; collateral history for patients who cannot report OTC use.
ask.title: Nephrotoxin and contrast exposure history (NSAID, ACEi/ARB, diuretic, aminoglycoside, vancomycin, PPI, iodinated contrast; timing)

ask.changes_what: Positive: hold/adjust the culprit, check orthostatic vitals, ECG, creatinine and electrolytes; negative: pursue arrhythmic, structural, vasovagal or infectious causes.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not accept a medication explanation as final in patients with exertional syncope, syncope while supine, palpitations preceding syncope, known structural heart disease or an abnormal ECG.
ask.escalation_warning: Bradycardia or high-grade AV block, QT prolongation, symptomatic hypotension with AKI, or opioid/sedative toxicity with reduced consciousness need monitored care and antidote/withdrawal decisions.
ask.how: Reconcile every drug (prescribed, OTC, herbal, recreational) against the pharmacy list: antihypertensives, diuretics, nitrates, alpha-blockers, PDE5 inhibitors, rate-slowing agents (beta-blockers, non-DHP CCB, digoxin), QT-prolonging drugs, sedatives/opioids, psychotropics, insulin/sulfonylureas, NSAIDs/ACEi/ARB/SGLT2i. Note start dates, dose changes and timing of the last dose versus the event.
ask.negative_finding: No culprit drug or no temporal relationship lowers the probability of medication effect but does not exclude intrinsic cardiac or neurological causes.
ask.pitfalls: Patients omit over-the-counter, recreational and 'as needed' drugs; drug effects are amplified by age, renal impairment, volume depletion and drug-drug interactions, so a long-standing drug can still be the cause after a change elsewhere. Attributing syncope to drugs without ECG review can miss conduction disease unmasked by the drug.
ask.positive_finding: A new or up-titrated vasoactive, rate-slowing, sedative or diuretic drug (or an intercurrent illness reducing intake/clearance) temporally linked to the event supports drug-induced orthostatic hypotension, bradyarrhythmia, hypovolemia/AKI or delirium.
ask.prerequisites: Access to an accurate medication list (pharmacy fill data, carer, containers); ask specifically about new drugs and dose escalations within the past 2-4 weeks.
ask.title: Antihypertensive / sedative / new-medication review (timing of last doses)

ask.changes_what: Positive: treat as significant volume loss - IV access, fluid/blood, search for bleeding source; negative: does not exclude moderate haemorrhage, use labs/other findings.
ask.contraindications: Do not stand a patient who is already hypotensive, in shock, or with suspected unstable spine/pelvic injury.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not attempt standing in patients who are hypotensive supine, obtunded, or at high fall risk; do not apply the volunteer-derived numbers uncritically to elderly patients on antihypertensives, beta-blockers or with autonomic neuropathy.
ask.escalation_warning: Inability to stand because of dizziness in a patient with suspected bleeding indicates large-volume loss: obtain large-bore access, type and crossmatch, and escalate immediately.

evidence.citation: McGee S, Abernethy WB 3rd, Simel DL. The rational clinical examination. Is this patient hypovolemic? JAMA. 1999;281(11):1022-1029.
evidence.population: Healthy adult volunteers undergoing phlebotomy (pooled RCE analysis of postural vital-sign studies)
evidence.quote: a much greater sensitivity for large blood loss of 97% (95% CI, 91%-100%); the corresponding specificity is 98% (95% CI, 97%-99%)
evidence.reference_standard: Known volume of blood removed by phlebotomy (before vs after)
evidence.target_condition: Hypovolaemia from LARGE acute blood loss (630-1150 mL) - finding: severe postural dizziness (preventing upright vitals) OR postural pulse increment >=30/min

evidence.citation: McGee S, Abernethy WB 3rd, Simel DL. The rational clinical examination. Is this patient hypovolemic? JAMA. 1999;281(11):1022-1029.
evidence.population: Healthy adult volunteers undergoing phlebotomy (pooled RCE analysis of postural vital-sign studies)
evidence.quote: The presence of either finding has a sensitivity for moderate blood loss of only 22% (95% confidence interval [CI], 6%-48%)
evidence.reference_standard: Known volume of blood removed by phlebotomy (before vs after)
evidence.target_condition: Hypovolaemia from MODERATE acute blood loss (450-630 mL) - finding: severe postural dizziness OR postural pulse increment >=30/min

ask.how: After supine vitals, stand the patient (with assistance) and ask about dizziness while measuring pulse and BP at about 1 minute. 'Severe' means dizziness so marked the patient cannot stay standing long enough for upright vitals or nearly faints; record it as a positive finding in its own right, together with any pulse increment of 30/min or more.
ask.negative_finding: Absence is reassuring only against large blood loss (sensitivity 0.97); after moderate (450-630 mL) loss the finding is usually absent (sensitivity 0.22), so a negative test does not exclude clinically important haemorrhage.
ask.pitfalls: Mild postural dizziness has no proven diagnostic value; supine tachycardia or hypotension is often absent even after 1 L loss. Evidence comes from healthy volunteers after phlebotomy, not from elderly or medicated ED patients, in whom baseline orthostatic symptoms are common.
ask.positive_finding: Severe postural dizziness (or a postural pulse increment >=30/min) is highly specific (0.98) for hypovolaemia from blood loss and is present in almost all subjects after large (630-1150 mL) blood loss.
ask.prerequisites: Supine rest for at least 2 minutes before standing; an assistant to prevent a fall. Sitting is not an adequate substitute for standing.
ask.title: Severe postural dizziness / inability to stand for vitals

ask.changes_what: Positive: stop the suspect drug, check urinalysis for pyuria/WBC casts and consider biopsy/steroids early; negative should not remove AIN from the differential of unexplained AKI on a new drug.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not use absence of fever/rash/arthralgia to exclude AIN, especially with PPIs or NSAIDs; do not attribute fever plus AKI to AIN without considering sepsis.
ask.escalation_warning: Rapidly rising creatinine, oliguria, or hyperkalemia on a suspect drug needs same-day nephrology review; biopsy decisions are time-sensitive because delayed drug withdrawal worsens recovery.
ask.how: Take a dated medication history for the preceding weeks to months (antibiotics, PPIs, NSAIDs, allopurinol, immune checkpoint inhibitors) and ask about fever, new rash, joint pains, and flank pain since starting; inspect the skin. Correlate the time course with the onset of creatinine rise.
ask.negative_finding: Absence of the triad is the rule: in biopsy series each feature is present in fewer than half of cases and the full triad in roughly 10%, so absence does not lower the probability of AIN meaningfully.
ask.pitfalls: PPI- and NSAID-induced AIN are typically oligosymptomatic with long latency; fever and rash after a new drug also occur with drug fever, DRESS, and infection without AIN. Definitive diagnosis requires kidney biopsy.
ask.positive_finding: Fever, rash, or arthralgia emerging after a new drug in a patient with unexplained AKI (often with sterile pyuria) supports drug-induced AIN and should prompt stopping the drug and nephrology input.
ask.prerequisites: Complete drug list including over-the-counter and recently stopped agents.
ask.title: Rash, fever, arthralgia after new drug (AIN triad)

examine.changes_what: Positive → catheterize/measure PVR now and seek the cause (drugs, prostate, cauda equina); negative with risk factors → bladder scan.
examine.contraindications: Avoid deep palpation over fresh lower abdominal incisions.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not use an absent suprapubic mass to exclude retention in AKI, delirium or suspected cauda equina — measure post-void residual.
examine.escalation_warning: Retention with new saddle anesthesia, leg weakness or back pain → emergent cauda equina evaluation (MRI).
examine.how: Patient supine: percuss from the umbilicus toward the pubis for a dome of suprapubic dullness and palpate for a smooth, tense, tender midline mass rising from the pelvis that provokes urge. Ask about LUTS, straining, dribbling, hematuria, prostate disease, anticholinergic/opioid use and time since last void; confirm with bladder scan or catheter volume.
examine.negative_finding: A non-palpable bladder does not exclude retention: obesity, smaller volumes and silent postoperative or opioid-related distension are missed. Obtain a bladder scan or post-void residual when retention is plausible.
examine.pitfalls: Postoperative bladder volume >500 mL was present in 44% at recovery-room discharge, and 54% of those without symptoms of distension could not void within 30 min (PMID 14977795, Abstract). Pelvic masses, pregnancy and ascites mimic; palpation cannot estimate volume.
examine.positive_finding: A palpable or percussible bladder above the pubis with inability to void indicates retention — catheterize and measure volume. This is a treatable cause of AKI, delirium and abdominal pain.
examine.prerequisites: Attempt to void first when able; know time of last void.
examine.title: Suprapubic palpation / percussion for distended bladder; LUTS and prostate history

examine.changes_what: Positive: emergency MRI whole lumbosacral spine/urgent spinal surgical referral. Negative: does not exclude cauda equina; if suspicion persists (bilateral sciatica, retention) still image.
examine.contraindications: Patient refusal; rectal exam may be deferred if imaging is already being obtained emergently, but perineal sensation should still be tested.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not use normal anal tone or perineal sensation to defer imaging when bilateral sciatica, new urinary retention or incontinence is present; the exam is insensitive for early cauda equina.
examine.escalation_warning: Any new saddle sensory change, sphincter disturbance or retention with back pain is a surgical emergency: emergent MRI and spinal referral without waiting for full deficit.
examine.how: With a chaperone and consent, test light touch and pinprick over the perineum, perianal skin, buttocks and inner thighs (S2-S5) comparing sides and asking about numbness when wiping; then digital rectal examination assessing resting anal tone, voluntary squeeze, and perianal sensation/anal wink. Pair with a bladder scan for post-void residual.
examine.negative_finding: Normal perineal sensation and anal tone do not exclude cauda equina compression - pooled sensitivities of individual red flags are only 0.19-0.43, and the diagnosis is often early or incomplete when sphincter signs are absent.
examine.pitfalls: Subjective perineal numbness is more sensitive than objective testing; anal tone is unreliable with prior anorectal surgery, chronic constipation or in the elderly. A large post-void residual (>500 mL) is the single most predictive bedside finding and should be checked with the exam.
examine.positive_finding: New saddle sensory loss or reduced anal tone in a patient with back pain and bilateral leg or sphincter symptoms is a red flag that mandates emergency MRI; pooled red flags for MRI-confirmed cauda equina are more specific (0.62-0.88) than sensitive.
examine.prerequisites: Chaperone, explanation and consent; document time of onset of bladder/bowel symptoms and bilateral leg symptoms.
examine.title: Saddle (perineal) sensory loss and reduced anal tone

examine.changes_what: CVA tenderness in a febrile patient with urinary symptoms supports pyelonephritis (culture, consider imaging for obstruction); its absence should not lower suspicion much.
examine.contraindications: Avoid fist percussion with suspected spinal fracture, recent flank surgery or known renal/splenic injury.
examine.do_not_use_when: Not validated in men, children, pregnancy, catheterized or elderly patients with nonspecific presentations; do not use to exclude obstruction or renal colic.
examine.escalation_warning: Flank tenderness with fever plus hypotension, AKI or a solitary/transplant kidney suggests obstructed pyelonephritis: urgent imaging and urology involvement.

examine.how: With the patient sitting or standing, place one palm flat over the costovertebral angle (below the 12th rib, lateral to the spine) and strike it with the ulnar side of the other fist, or press firmly with the fingertips. Compare both sides and watch the face for wincing; ask if the pain is the same as their presenting pain.
examine.negative_finding: Absence of CVA tenderness barely changes the probability (absence of back pain LR 0.8) and does not exclude pyelonephritis, especially in elderly or immunocompromised patients.
examine.pitfalls: Musculoskeletal back pain, rib injury and retrocecal appendicitis cause false positives; the RCE LRs are for uncomplicated UTI in women, not for separating pyelonephritis from cystitis or for renal colic.
examine.positive_finding: Unilateral CVA tenderness modestly increases the probability of urinary tract infection in symptomatic women (LR+ 1.7, 95% CI 1.1-2.5) and, with fever, points toward pyelonephritis rather than cystitis.
examine.prerequisites: Warn the patient first; assess before analgesia if possible.
examine.title: Costovertebral angle (flank) tenderness

examine.changes_what: Positive: emergency whole-spine MRI, dexamethasone if malignancy suspected, spinal/oncology referral. Negative in suspected GBS: pursue neuromuscular workup; retained UMN signs argue against GBS.
examine.contraindications: None; in acute spinal shock reflexes may be absent below the level for days, so hyporeflexia does not exclude cord compression.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not rely on absent hyperreflexia or a normal plantar response to exclude acute cord compression, and do not delay imaging to complete a detailed sensory map.
examine.escalation_warning: New bilateral leg weakness, a sensory level, or new bladder dysfunction in a patient with known cancer is metastatic spinal cord compression until MRI proves otherwise; outcome depends on ambulatory status at treatment, so image within hours.
examine.how: Test pinprick and light touch moving upward from the feet on the trunk to find a dermatome above which sensation becomes normal; confirm with temperature (cold tuning fork). Test knee and ankle reflexes, clonus, and the plantar response by stroking the lateral sole from heel toward the toes with a blunt object; check bladder with a post-void residual.
examine.negative_finding: Absence of a sensory level or of upper motor neuron signs does not exclude early cord compression, because acute lesions can present with flaccidity and areflexia (spinal shock) and sensory levels are often imprecise; in GBS reflexes are lost and no level is found.
examine.pitfalls: The Babinski sign has only fair inter-rater reliability (kappa 0.30) and agreed with known upper motor neuron weakness in just 56% of examinations; withdrawal from a ticklish sole mimics an extensor response. The clinical level often lies several segments below the true lesion, so image the whole spine.
examine.positive_finding: A bilateral sensory level on the trunk with hyperreflexia, clonus, or extensor plantars below it localizes to the spinal cord and, with back pain in a patient with cancer, indicates metastatic cord compression until MRI proves otherwise.
examine.prerequisites: Cooperative patient able to report sensation; know dermatome landmarks (T4 nipple, T10 umbilicus, L1 inguinal); compare bilaterally.
examine.title: Sensory level with hyperreflexia / extensor plantar (Babinski) below the level
